Nez Perce. The Nimiipuu, meaning "the People," are a Plateau nation historically inhabiting the Pacific Northwest of present-day Oregon, Washington, and Idaho. They are renowned for their salmon fisheries, distinctive appaloosa horse breeding, and Chief Joseph's legendary resistance and retreat across over one thousand miles during the Nez Perce War of 1877.

The Nez Perce are a Sahaptian-speaking people, and their name in French, meaning "Pierced Nose," may derive from a misunderstanding, since they did not universally practice nose piercing. They developed sophisticated salmon-fishing economies along Columbia River tributaries, constructing sophisticated weirs and preservation techniques, and they gathered roots and hunted game. They bred distinctive appaloosa horses, known for their spotted coats and endurance, and mastered mounted hunting and warfare through equestrian skills unmatched in the region.

Chief Joseph, known in his own language as Hinmaton-Yalaktit, led the Wallowa band's desperate resistance when forced from their ancestral Wallowa Valley. During the Nez Perce War of 1877, they retreated over one thousand one hundred miles toward Canada, repeatedly defeating pursuing U.S. forces before surrender near the Canadian border. Joseph's surrender speech—"I will fight no more forever"—became iconic. He was exiled to Oklahoma, then Kansas, before finally allowed to return to the Colville Reservation in Washington.

Today the Nez Perce Nation is based on the Nez Perce Reservation in north-central Idaho, where language revitalization and traditional cultural practices continue.
